sections.text: A trait bound limits a generic type to types that have a certain trait. You write it after the type parameter: T: Display means "any type T that implements Display". Inside the function you can then use everything Display gives you, such as {} in println!.

use std::fmt::Display; brings the name Display into scope, the same way use std::collections::HashMap; did for HashMap. Without the bound, println! with {value} would not compile, because Rust cannot know that every T can be shown. If you call the function with a type that has no Display, the call fails with error E0277 (the trait bound is not satisfied).
Use + to require several traits at once. This function needs T to be comparable and printable:
When there are many bounds, the signature gets crowded. A where clause moves them after the signature, with the same meaning:
(use std::fmt::{Debug, Display}; imports two names in one line.) Debug is the trait behind {:?}, and Clone is the trait with the clone method.

There are two shortcuts for traits. In an argument, impl Trait means "some type that has this trait". It is shorthand for a generic with a bound. In a return type, it says "I return some type with this trait" without naming it. The function still returns one concrete type:

(struct Dog; is a struct with no fields at all. You create one by just writing Dog.) A function returning impl Speak cannot return a Dog in one branch and a Robot in another: the compiler needs one real type (error E0308 otherwise). Mixing types in one collection is solved with Box<dyn Trait> in Unit 10.

Many traits are so common that Rust can write the impl for you. Put #[derive(...)] above a struct or enum and list the traits. Debug lets you print with {:?}. Clone adds a clone method. PartialEq lets you compare with == and !=. Copy makes values copy instead of move (every field must be Copy too). Default gives a default value, such as 0 for numbers.
A bound is like a requirement in a job listing: "anyone who can do X and Y may apply". The compiler checks that every type you pass meets it, so mistakes show up as compile errors, not crashes.

T: Trait is Java's <T extends Comparable<T>>, C++20's concepts, or a Go constraint. impl Trait in an argument position is generic sugar: you can't name the type, so use <T: Trait> when two arguments must be the same type (a: T, b: T). Note that derive(PartialEq) compares field by field, like a Java record's equals.

exercise.prompt: show takes only an i32. Make it work for any type that can be printed: add use std::fmt::Display; at the top, and change the signature to fn show<T: Display>(item: T). Then add show("hi"); at the end of main. It should print two lines: <5> and <hi>.

quiz.question: What does fn f<T: Display + Clone>(x: T) require of T?
options: T must implement both Display and Clone
T must implement Display or Clone

quiz.question: What does #[derive(Debug)] do?
options: It turns on debug mode for the program
It asks the compiler to write the Debug impl, so {:?} works
It prints the struct when it is created

quiz.question: Can fn make() -> impl Speak return a Dog in one branch and a Robot in another?
options: Yes, any type with Speak is allowed
Yes, but only inside an if
No, it must always return one concrete type
